Joy as teacher celebrates graduation in hospital
items.description: Graduate pleasantly surprised in hospital after missing graduation ceremony.
content: Joyce Owenda Omondi, a Bachelor of Education Arts in English Literature graduate of Kaimosi Friends University, celebrates her graduation at Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital in Kisumu after missing the university's graduation ceremony due to illness.
On Friday, as scores of graduands streamed into Kaimosi Friends University, Vihiga, ready for the much-awaited conferment, Ms Joyce Owenda Omondi was not one of them.
Instead, the newly minted English and literature teacher sat on her hospital bed at the Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital, waiting for her family members.
A few minutes to noon, her parents, three sisters, a brother, in-laws and several nephews and nieces arrived at the hospital.

The nurses allowed Ms Owenda to step out of Ward Eight, which had now become her temporary home. She was dressed in her graduation gown which her elder brother, Mr Benedict Wanga, had brought for her.
“My brother had gone an extra mile, he travelled to my university and collected my graduation gown. This was a whole surprise,” she said.
For hours, the family members sang, danced, laughed and shared a meal with Ms Owenda. Thereafter, the family members gave their speeches. Ms Owenda, 24, also shared her experience at the hospital.
Read: What every varsity student should do before graduation
Before leaving, the family members shared a cake, held prayers, and took photographs.
“I am very happy. This is something I really wanted despite the sickness. My family members made the day beautiful,” a beaming Ms Owenda said.
This, however, was not the kind of graduation she had hoped for after completing her final exams in April this year.
Ms Owenda said she joined university in 2021, but deferred her studies to the following year due to lack of school fees. She made friends with other students with similar fees problems.

“By the time we got to our fourth year, we would jokingly refer to ourselves as fifth year students because we had all deferred our studies,” she said, adding that they had planned to take a group photo during their graduation to remind them of a journey of resilience.
“Graduation was a big deal to me; not even once did I ever think of missing out for any reason,” Ms Owenda said.

Joyce Owenda Omondi, a Bachelor of Education Arts in English Literature graduate of Kaimosi Friends University, celebrates her graduation at Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Teaching and Referral Hospital in Kisumu after missing the university's graduation ceremony due to illness.
However, in October she started feeling sickly, with symptoms including dizziness, loss of appetite and fatigue.
Her brother, Mr Wanga, said the symptoms had first appeared in 2025 but disappeared before she could be diagnosed.
When the symptoms reappeared, a month before graduation, Ms Owenda went to Jaramogi Oginga Odinga Hospital where she was told she had low blood supply.
Later on, further tests revealed she had Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), also known as Lupus, a chronic autoimmune disease in which the body’s immune system attacks healthy tissues.
She, however, did not lose hope; each time a doctor came to check up on her, she would ask if there was any possibility of attending the graduation ceremony.

The doctors, however, said it was risky for her to step out of the hospital unless an ambulance would drop her at the institution, stay by in case of an emergency, and later bring her back to the facility.
The doctors and nurses had also hinted that the celebrations could as well be held at the facility.
Read: Why Kenyan graduates struggle to find employment
Mr Wanga had gone ahead to consult with the hospital administration, who allowed them to hold the celebrations at the hospital.

“I was unable to join my friends to take our planned photos since they were at the graduation grounds while I stayed in hospital. I am, however, glad that I got to experience the joy of graduation,” Ms Owenda said.
Her brother, Mr Wanga, said what mattered to the family was to put a smile on his sister’s face. They plan to hold a thanksgiving ceremony when she leaves the hospital.
“The hospital put in place all the necessary arrangements to ensure the celebration was a success,” said Mr Wanga.
The doctors, Ms Owenda says, have not only been counselling and guiding her on how to manage the condition, including routine checkups.
The 24-year-old is now hopeful that if all goes well, she will be discharged next week.

Judge orders prisons reforms after inmate was killed with smuggled hammer
items.description: Justice Magare says authorities failed in their duty to protect the prisoner.
content: Inmates are escorted into Nakuru Main Prison on April 20, 2026.

The High Court has recommended sweeping security reforms in Kenya's prisons, including mandatory searches of inmates returning from work, tighter control of workshop tools, CCTV surveillance and improved emergency access to locked cells, following the killing of an inmate at Nyeri Maximum Security Prison.

Justice Kizito Magare directed the Kenya Prisons Service to account for measures taken to prevent dangerous tools and other contraband from reaching inmates' sleeping quarters following the death of Shem Mugendi Kariuki, who was attacked with a hammer by a fellow prisoner in August 2015.

The court ordered the Prisons Service to file, within 120 days, an affidavit sworn by an officer of at least the rank of Deputy Commissioner General, detailing measures currently in place to control and account for tools used in prison industries and workshops.

The judge recommended that every inmate returning from work undergo a search before entering accommodation blocks and that prison authorities introduce proper systems for accounting for tools at the end of working hours.
He also said walk-through metal detectors should be installed at entry points to workshops and accommodation blocks in maximum-security facilities.
However, the searches must respect inmates' dignity and decency and be conducted by officers of the same sex, as required under the Persons Deprived of Liberty Act.
This photograph dated August 27, 2016 shows inmates at Naivasha Maximum Security Prison. PHOTO | FILE | NATION MEDIA GROUP

The court further recommended installing closed-circuit television cameras in corridors and common areas, improving supervision of accommodation blocks and conducting intelligence-led searches for mobile phones and other prohibited items.
It also called for confidential reporting mechanisms through which inmates can alert prison officers to threats, disputes and potential violence.
The recommendations followed findings that the ward's inmate in charge and another prisoner knew of a dispute between Kariuki and his assailant before the killing.
The judge said prison authorities should review emergency response procedures to ensure officers can gain controlled access to locked accommodation wards when lives are at risk.
In Kariuki's case, night sentries could not immediately access the ward, with several minutes passing before the door was opened.

The court also recommended that every death in prison custody be subjected to a prompt, independent and effective investigation, with the deceased's family informed in writing of the circumstances and findings.
It called for the full operationalisation of the National Coroners Service Act, 2017, and the publication of annual statistics on deaths in custody.

The judge further urged Parliament and the Prisons Service to complete the review of the Prisons Act, 1962, and the Prisons Rules to align them with the 2010 Constitution and the Persons Deprived of Liberty Act.
Inmates are escorted into Nakuru Main Prison on April 20, 2026.

"In particular, the duty to protect inmates from violence by other inmates, tool and contraband control, and the investigation of deaths in custody should be placed on a clear statutory footing," the judge said.
The court also directed that every prison establishment and the Prisons Service headquarters have a designated information officer to handle requests from families of inmates who die in custody.

The Deputy Registrar was directed to transmit the judgment to the Commissioner General of Prisons, the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights and the Commission on Administrative Justice for their attention to the recommendations.
The reforms followed a petition by Faith Muthoni Kariuki, whose 35-year-old son was killed while serving a 15-year prison sentence.
According to court records, Peter Hiuhu Gachau, alias Undertaker, attacked Kariuki on August 16, 2015, while he was sleeping in Block B, Ward 7.

The court heard that Gachau, who was serving a death sentence for robbery with violence, stole a claw hammer from the prison carpentry workshop, concealed it under his clothes and smuggled it into the ward.
He told investigators that he believed Kariuki had stolen Sh27,000 from his mobile money account.
Gachau struck Kariuki twice on the head before strangling him. He was later sentenced to 35 years in prison.
Justice Magare faulted prison officers for failing to account for tools after work and search inmates before allowing them back into their sleeping quarters.

The court rejected the State's argument that the killing was an independent criminal act by a fellow inmate, ruling that prison authorities had a constitutional duty to protect Kariuki's life and security.
It noted that the ward housed 95 high-risk inmates, many of whom slept on the floor, increasing the risk of violence.
The judge also found that Gachau had been secretly operating a mobile phone inside the prison, which was recovered from another ward after the killing.

The court agreed with lawyer John Mwariri that the government's failure to respond to a letter seeking information on measures taken to ensure prisoners' safety violated the mother's right of access to information under Article 35(1)(a) of the Constitution.
Through Mwariri, Faith Muthoni Kariuki had moved to court seeking compensation, arguing that the State had failed to protect her son while he was in its exclusive custody.
Mr Mwariri submitted that the government had failed to respond to a letter dated May 28, 2025, seeking information on measures taken to enhance prisoners' safety.
The court found that the failure to respond violated her constitutional right of access to information and awarded her Sh2.5 million in compensation.

items.title: Gachagua gives Mt Kenya leaders Christmas deadline to dump Ruto, promises political direction
items.description: Gachagua has given Mt Kenya leaders still supporting President William Ruto until Christmas to reconsider their political loyalties, warning that the region will decide its political direction during family gatherings.
content: NAIROBI, Kenya, Nov 22 – Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has warned Mt Kenya leaders still supporting President William Ruto that they risk being rejected by voters in the 2027 General Election, saying the region will settle its political direction during the Christmas festivities.

Gachagua said political decisions in the Mt Kenya region are traditionally made during family gatherings over Christmas, when relatives return home and deliberate on the leaders they want to represent them.

Speaking in Embu County, the Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) leader said discussions held between December 23 and December 26 would determine the political fate of leaders seeking elective positions in the region.
He warned politicians who have remained in Ruto’s camp despite growing political differences with the former Deputy President to reconsider their positions before the festive season.

“Here in the mountain, let me tell those who don’t know: when we go to the election next year, every five years, decisions here in the mountain are made during Christmas. Starting from December 23, 24, 25, by the 26th on Boxing Day, the decision is concluded,” Gachagua said.

items.title: John Njue pledges KSh100M for Edwin Sifuna US campaign
items.description: Edwin Sifuna receives KSh100M diaspora pledge in New Jersey
content: Embu-born diaspora resident drives nine hours to New Jersey engagement to back Nairobi Senator’s 2027 bid

John Njue, a Kenyan diaspora resident originally from Embu County living in the United States, has pledged KSh100 million towards Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s 2027 presidential campaign under the Linda Mwananchi Movement. Njue made the commitment yesterday during Sifuna’s diaspora engagement in New Jersey, where he revealed that he had driven for nine hours to attend the meeting and declare his financial and political support.

Addressing supporters gathered at the forum, Njue stated that members of the Kenyan diaspora were prepared to mobilise resources for Sifuna’s political agenda without requiring the Nairobi Senator to seek external borrowing. Speaking in a mix of English and Kiswahili during the session, Njue affirmed his personal commitment to the campaign alongside fellow Kenyans living abroad.

“I have driven for nine hours to come and be with you. We will give you KSh100 million for your campaign,” Njue, a United States-based businessman hailing from Embu, told the meeting. He further urged the Linda Mwananchi Movement leadership to establish a transparent, formal channel for receiving diaspora contributions and expressed interest in future public-private partnerships to deliver development projects once a new administration takes office.

Sifuna, who also serves as the Linda Mwananchi Movement party leader, arrived in the United States on November 21 to launch a multi-state diaspora outreach tour scheduled to run through early December. Responding to the pledge, Sifuna welcomed the diaspora backing and emphasised the importance of transparency and accountability in managing public and campaign resources

The New Jersey forum marks the opening leg of Sifuna’s United States itinerary, which includes the launch of a diaspora coordination office in Hackettstown, New Jersey, followed by town hall meetings and community engagements across Allentown in Pennsylvania, the Washington DC, Maryland and Virginia region, Texas, Washington State, and California ahead of the 2027 General Election.

Development Is Not Charity: Taxation, Patronage and the Politics of Power in Kenya
items.description: Development is not a presidential gift; it is a public obligation funded by the labour and taxes of the people. Yet Kenya’s political landscape increasingly presents public development as the personal…
content: Development is not a presidential gift; it is a public obligation funded by the labour and taxes of the people. Yet Kenya’s political landscape increasingly presents public development as the personal generosity of President William Ruto, who travels across the country announcing projects in ways that often blur the distinction between public responsibility and electoral mobilisation.

From a historical materialist perspective, this is not merely a question of political rhetoric but of power, ownership and the distribution of public resources. The state collects taxes from workers, peasants, traders and businesses across the country. These resources are pooled into the national treasury and must serve the collective needs of the population, not the electoral interests of an individual or political faction.

Walter Rodney, in his final speech, Sign of the Times, delivered on 6 June 1980, challenged the separation of material needs from political rights. His argument that access to milk and constitutional freedom were inseparable reminds us that material conditions and political power are interconnected. In Kenya, access to roads, hospitals, water, schools and electricity cannot be reduced to presidential generosity; these are necessities financed through collective taxation and owed to the people.

The politics of announcing projects during presidential tours risks reproducing a patronage system in which communities are encouraged to associate public investment with political loyalty. Development then becomes a political currency, used to cultivate support, consolidate power and influence electoral outcomes. This obscures the fact that taxpayers are financing these projects in the first place.

The contradiction is particularly glaring in a country where taxation continues to burden ordinary citizens amid rising living costs. Workers and small businesses contribute to the public purse, yet they are often politically positioned as beneficiaries of the very resources they collectively generate. Such a narrative reinforces the illusion that development flows from the generosity of political leaders rather than from the productive labour and financial contributions of society.

Development should not be a reward for voting for the ruling party, attending presidential rallies or endorsing a re-election campaign. It must be guided by public need, equitable distribution, transparency and democratic accountability.
The struggle, therefore, is not simply over which region receives a road or a water project. It is about challenging the politics of patronage that turns public obligations into political favours.
The President is not the benefactor of the people; he is the custodian of public resources. Development is not charity. It is the people’s right.

Wachira Nyaga is a cadre of the Revolutionary Socialist League, a Founding Member of Social Justice Movement Kenya, a member of Kenya Organic Intellectuals, and the Founder of Embu Community Justice Center. His work focuses on political education, community organising, social justice, African liberation, and the relationship between theory and practice.

items.title: Opposition within opposition? How third power bloc is taking shape ahead of 2027 elections
items.description: Gachagua and Matiang’i have in recent days traded barbs.
content: From left: Jubilee leader Fred Matiang’i, People’s Party of Kenya leader Ndindi Nyoro, People’s Liberation Party chief Martha Karua, and Siaya Governor James Orengo.
For some time now, the country has been treated to two main political factions; one supporting President William Ruto and his re-election bid, and another, an amalgamation of his opponents.
However, a new centre is slowly emerging that appears to be splintering from the second grouping with the potential to significantly redraw the political landscape ahead of the polls on August 10.

The growing partnership between Jubilee presidential candidate Fred Matiang’i, People’s Party of Kenya leader Ndindi Nyoro, People’s Liberation Party chief Martha Karua, and Siaya Governor James Orengo, is one of the most significant developments in the opposition’s succession politics so far.
Jubilee Party leader Dr Fred Matiang’i joined by Ndindi Nyoro, Martha Karua and Siaya Governor James Orengo amongst other leaders during a joint People's Tour in Kisii town on November 15, 2026.

Their joint political activities, which have culminated in a high-profile tour of the Gusii region, have fuelled speculation that the four are forming a powerful political bloc that could influence the direction of the opposition and the selection of its presidential candidate.

On Sunday, November 22, 2026, the leaders are expected to attend a service at Kiang’ombe Anglican Church in Ms Karua’s home county of Kirinyaga, before holding a series of rallies and political engagements as they step up their efforts to consolidate support across the country.

While the leaders have publicly presented their collaboration as a strategy to increase the opposition’s national presence, insiders claim that the alliance was formed in response to the “arrogance” of certain opposition leaders, who, they say, could jeopardise the opposition’s collective quest for the presidency.
Also Read: Broad-based cracks: UDA-ODM tensions simmer amid Ruto Gusii tour
Dr Fred Matiang’i and Rigathi Gachagua during the United Opposition's tour of Kisumu.

The former Deputy President and Dr Matiang’i have in recent days traded barbs, further exposing the widening political fault lines within the opposition over its leadership and strategy ahead of the 2027 elections.

Wiper Patriotic Front spokesperson Ndegwa Njiru has cautioned that the opposition coalition remains fragile, urging its principals to treat one another with respect and rein in their supporters to avoid undermining the partnership.

“Those joking around with this relationship must understand that it is very delicate and should be treated with the utmost respect. It is important that you rein in your supporters and ensure they respect other presidential candidates,” Mr Njiru told the opposition principals.

According to experts, the implications of the Matiang’i-Nyoro-Karua-Orengo alliance must be considered in light of Kenya’s constitutional requirement that a presidential candidate has to secure 50 per cent plus one of all votes cast in order to be declared the winner in the first round.

Therefore, the emerging political partnership could have a broader significance: its influence could affect how votes are distributed among competing presidential candidates, potentially making it difficult for any one candidate to reach the constitutional threshold.

If the alliance attracts a significant proportion of voters who would otherwise support different opposition groups, it could lead to a fragmented presidential contest and increase the likelihood of a second round.
Siaya Governor James Orengo at his Ugenya home in Siaya County, on February 27, 2026.

Advocate Chris Omore says that this developing alliance is important because it could complicate the arithmetic of the presidential contest by preventing any candidate from achieving the required number of votes to win in the first round.

“This alliance is crucial because it has the potential to deny any presidential candidate the 50 per cent-plus-one threshold. Its impact will be felt in how votes are distributed across the political formations, particularly if it operates independently of the other opposition groups,” said Mr Omore.

Article 138(4) of the Constitution provides that a presidential candidate must receive more than half of all votes cast in the election and at least 25 per cent of the votes cast in each of more than half of the 47 counties. This translates to at least 24 counties. Article 138(5) further provides that where no candidate meets these two conditions, a fresh election must be held within 30 days, involving the candidate who received the greatest number of votes and the one who received the second-greatest number.
The Constitution thus provides for a two-candidate run-off rather than allowing a candidate to win simply by polling more votes than their competitors.

Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi, a member of Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement has expressed confidence that the opposition will eventually rally behind a single presidential candidate ahead of the 2027 General Election, drawing parallels with the 2002 political alliance that ended Kanu’s 24-year rule.
Also Read: Bring it on - Uhuru’s push for opposition unity opens new battlefront with Ruto
He maintained that despite the current realignments and competing interests, opposition leaders would eventually overcome their differences and settle on one candidate to challenge President Ruto.
“The opposition will have one candidate like in 2002 because the concerns are the same. We are confident we shall have a 2002 moment,” Mr Osotsi said.

But despite his explanation, everything points to the fact that all is not well within the united opposition, with some members feeling sidelined because they do not have as high a number of registered voters from their own backyards as others do. It is this feeling that is said to fuel the need for a third force: an alternative alliance.

The Matiang’i-Nyoro-Karua-Orengo partnership stands out, with analysts noting that the four leaders have raised concerns over the management and direction of the opposition, suggesting that they could be charting an independent political path outside the existing power matrix.

Dr Matiang’i has, however, dismissed suggestions that the emerging partnership represents a breakaway faction or an attempt to undermine other opposition leaders, insisting that the arrangement is part of a collective strategy to strengthen the coalition.

Speaking to Sunday Nation, the former Interior Cabinet Secretary said opposition leaders had agreed that politicians should organise separate activities across the country instead of concentrating their mobilisation efforts in one geographical area.
“We all agreed in opposition that everybody moves around. We need to create teams to cover the whole country,” he said.
He suggested that the growing speculation surrounding the leaders’ movements was being fuelled by unnecessary political interpretations.
“People just over-read things,” he said. “We all understand the country. We must all move, at some point sit and sort out the underlying issues.”
Jubilee Party leader Fred Matiang’i addresses residents of Kware in Ongata Rongai, Kajiado County on October 25, 2026.
Dr Matiang’i’s presidential ambitions have increasingly gained visibility through his engagements with leaders from different political backgrounds.

Pundits say that the former Interior CS brings national government experience, having served in several Cabinet portfolios under former President Uhuru Kenyatta. His supporters see his administrative experience and national profile as important assets in a contest against an incumbent seeking a second term.
Also Read: Their silent fears - What's keeping opposition chiefs awake in 2027 poll plan
However, his political challenge is transforming that profile into a broad electoral coalition capable of attracting support beyond his Gusii backyard.
“Nyoro’s involvement is particularly significant because it gives the emerging partnership a foothold in the politically influential Mt Kenya region,” says political analyst Geoffrey Mboya.

“Karua, on the other hand, brings a different proposition to the emerging alliance. The former Justice Minister and longtime reform campaigner has maintained a national political profile built around governance, constitutionalism and accountability. She has also previously vied for the presidency and was Raila Odinga’s running mate in the last election, making her participation in the partnership important in the management of competing ambitions,” says Mr Mboya.
During the Gusii gathering, Ms Karua sought to demonstrate that individual aspirations would not stand in the way of a collective political project.
Also Read: Drama as Sifuna, Gachagua, Kalonzo, Maraga, others walk out of key IEBC meeting

“We are here with Dr Fred Matiang’i, Ndindi Nyoro and James Orengo. Many of us, including myself, have presidential ambitions. However, if it is agreed that Dr Matiang’i should be the flag bearer, I will step aside and support him,” she said. She extended the same commitment to Mr Nyoro, saying she would support him if the opposition settled on his candidature.
Her remarks were an important political signal at a time when the opposition’s biggest challenge could be managing the competing ambitions of its leading figures.
Governor Orengo’s appearance alongside Dr Matiang’i, Ms Karua and Mr Nyoro in Gusii, pundits say, also carries significance beyond a routine political engagement.

Mr Orengo had previously aligned himself with Nairobi Senator Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement. However, his recent political activities, including the acquisition of the Liberal Democratic Party and public endorsement of Dr Matiang’i in Kisii, have placed him increasingly within the emerging partnership.
During the Gusii rally, Mr Orengo openly urged the community to support Dr Matiang’i’s presidential ambitions, invoking the political legacy of Raila and his father, Jaramogi Oginga Odinga.

“I thank the Abagusii people for consistently voting for the late Raila Odinga. And not only Raila, but also the late Jaramogi Oginga Odinga. Please understand that if you vote for President Ruto to return to office, Raila will not be pleased wherever he may be. However, if you vote for your son, Matiang’i, he will be very happy,” he told residents.

items.title: Kenya’s small farmers feed the nation but are losing the battle
items.description: Kenya's smallholder farmers face climate change, cartels, and high input costs. Sarah Mutio examines the crisis and the solutions needed to fix it.
content: From climate shocks to exploitative cartels, Kenya’s smallholder farmers face a perfect storm — and without urgent intervention, the country’s food security hangs in the balance.
Kenya’s agricultural sector feeds millions, drives the economy, and sustains entire communities — yet the very farmers who make this possible are being left behind.

Agriculture is the backbone of Kenya’s economy. More than 70 per cent of Kenyans living in rural areas depend on farming for food and income, most of them smallholder families cultivating land by hand, selling modest surpluses, and hoping the rains arrive on time. For these families, farming is not a livelihood choice — it is survival. It puts food on the table, pays school fees, and keeps households afloat in an economy where formal employment remains out of reach for most. Beyond the household, agriculture feeds industry. Tea factories, sugar mills, cotton processors, and food manufacturers all draw their raw materials from Kenya’s farms. The government, in turn, taxes these industries, channelling revenue into roads, schools, and public services. The chain is long and the stakes are high.
Yet for all its importance, farming in Kenya is in crisis — and the people bearing the heaviest burden are the smallholders who do the most work and earn the least reward.

Climate change has fundamentally altered the rhythms that generations of Kenyan farmers relied upon. Rainfall patterns have become unpredictable. Prolonged droughts wipe out entire harvests. Flash floods destroy crops overnight. Farmers who once planted by the calendar now plant by guesswork, and many lose everything. Most Kenyans, it should be noted, combine farming with other work — tending a small shamba alongside a job in town or a business in the market — which means that when harvests fail, the financial blow ripples through entire households and communities.

Equally damaging is the stranglehold of middlemen and cartels. At harvest time, brokers descend on farms and buy produce at exploitatively low prices. They warehouse it, wait for scarcity to push prices up, and then sell at a premium — pocketing profits that should, by rights, belong to the farmer who planted, tended, and harvested the crop. The farmer works; the middleman earns. This cycle has persisted for decades, and it has kept smallholders poor.

The cost of farm inputs compounds the problem. Seeds, fertiliser, agrochemicals, and equipment have become prohibitively expensive, partly due to taxation and importation costs. Many farmers cannot afford mechanisation and fall back on hand hoes and traditional methods that limit both productivity and income. Meanwhile, cheap imported produce — often subsidised in its country of origin — floods Kenyan markets and undercuts local farmers who cannot compete on price. Small-scale producers are squeezed from every direction: high costs of production, low sale prices, and foreign competition they have no tools to fight.

There are also tensions closer to home. In many parts of Kenya, conflict between crop farmers and pastoralists is a recurring and destructive reality. Livestock straying onto cultivated land destroys harvests and ignites bitter disputes between neighbours, sometimes with lasting consequences for community relations and farm productivity.
None of these challenges are insurmountable. Solutions exist, but they require coordinated commitment from farmers, government, and the broader community.

Irrigation must replace dependence on rainfall. The government has the technical capacity to expand irrigation infrastructure and the responsibility to do so urgently. Alongside this, farmers should be supported to adopt drought-resistant crop varieties and given timely, accurate weather forecasts via radio and mobile platforms — tools that are affordable and already widely accessible.

Cooperative farming offers the most practical antidote to middlemen and cartels. When farmers sell collectively, they negotiate from strength. Cooperatives can also pool resources to purchase inputs at wholesale prices, reducing individual costs significantly. Organic manure — readily available on most smallholder farms — can substitute for expensive chemical fertiliser, cutting costs further while improving soil health.

The government must do its part on trade policy. Meaningful protection for local farmers — through controlled imports and reduced input taxes — would level a playing field that is currently tilted heavily against the smallholder. At the same time, farmers need training and support to improve product quality: better packaging, grading, and processing that command higher market prices and open doors to formal retail and export markets.

Technology is already transforming farming for those who can access it. Mobile phones allow farmers to monitor weather, track market prices, and sell directly to buyers without intermediaries. Mechanisation, where affordable, dramatically increases productivity. The government and development partners must work together to close the gap between farmers who have access to these tools and the many who do not.

Kenya’s small-scale farmers are not a charity case. They are the foundation of the country’s food system, its rural economy, and its social fabric. They deserve policy that protects them, markets that reward them, and a government that takes their challenges as seriously as their contribution.
If Kenya is to feed itself in the decades ahead, it must start by ensuring the people who grow the food can afford to keep farming.

items.description: Former Nation Media Group journalist Mohamed Ahmed has been named among Kenya’s 100 Most Influential Muslims for 2026, recognised for business leadership.

Mombasa - Mohamed Ahmed, a former journalist with Nation Media Group who now leads sales operations at a Mombasa-based real estate firm, has been named among Kenya's 100 Most Influential and Inspirational Muslims for 2026.

The recognition, organised by The Muslim Media, placed Ahmed in the Business & Management category, acknowledging his contributions following a career that spans journalism, communications, marketing and business development.

Ahmed spent six years at Nation Media Group, where he reported on security and political affairs across Kenya's Coast Region.

That grounding in public affairs and stakeholder communication later shaped his transition into corporate roles, eventually leading him to his current position as Head of Sales at Megna Homes.

The company is a Mombasa-based property developer active in residential development, project management, sales and property management. Its flagship project, Santana in Mtopanga, is a gated community comprising 816 residential units and 64 commercial spaces. In 2025, Santana became the first development by a Mombasa-based real estate firm to receive EDGE certification for sustainable design.
Speaking after receiving the award, Ahmed described the recognition as a prompt for continued responsibility rather than a personal accolade.

He also credited Megna Homes for the platform the role has provided him.

The awards programme recognised individuals across a broad range of categories, including Lifetime Achievement, Media, Law and Academia, Daawah, Food, Fashion and Arts, Leadership, Community Service, STEM, and Business and Entrepreneurship.

"No other way": CS Murkomen issues new order ahead of police recruitment
items.description: Kipchumba Murkomen warns job seekers against paying bribes as Kenya’s December 10 police recruitment promises public results and observers at 423 centres.
content: Search option is now available at TUKO! Feel free to search the content on topics/people you enjoy reading about in the top right corner ;)

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has urged Kenyans not to dispose of land or other assets to fund bribes for police jobs, warning that the upcoming recruitment exercise will be conducted transparently and that anyone involved in irregularities will face stern consequences.

Murkomen made the remarks on Saturday, November 21, while speaking at the Amaya Youth Empowerment Initiative in Tiaty, Baringo County. His message came two days after the National Police Service (NPS) formally opened applications for the constable intake scheduled for Thursday, December 10.

"We have announced police recruitment. It will be fair and transparent. We don't want corruption in it," he said.
Murkomen's Warning to Families and Brokers
The CS directed his caution squarely at young people from poor and rural backgrounds, who are frequently targeted by brokers promising guaranteed placement in exchange for money.

"No one should sell their land or other property to raise money for bribe. We will invite observers to recruitment centres. When the recruitment ends all who did not make it should be informed right there," he said.

Murkomen further instructed the NPS to publicly announce the names of successful candidates at each centre so that independent observers and members of the public can verify the outcome. He added that gender representation must be factored into the process.

"There is no shortcut. It will be done transparently to ensure those who qualify are recruited and those who don't are informed immediately. And gender must also be considered so that our girls also get in," he said.

The NPS has separately warned the public against paying anyone who promises a guaranteed spot, noting that the exercise is free and that corruption and the submission of false information during recruitment are criminal offences. The service urged anyone aware of suspected malpractice to report it at the nearest police station.
Opiyo Wandayi says opposition has sensed defeat after storming out of IEBC meeting
December Recruitment: What Applicants Should Know
The NPS recruitment notice, issued on November 19, states that the exercise will run from 8am to 5pm on December 10 at 423 designated centres nationwide, and candidates must arrive by 8am.

Eligible applicants must be Kenyan citizens aged between 18 and 28, hold a valid national identity card, and have attained at least a D+ in KCSE, including a D+ in English or Kiswahili. Physical requirements are a minimum height of 5 ft 8 in for men and 5 ft 3 in for women, and candidates must be medically fit with no criminal record. Female candidates must not be pregnant at the time of recruitment or during training.

Application forms are available through the NPS, Kenya Police , Administration Police and DCI websites, as well as at Huduma Centres, and candidates are required to present both originals and copies of their documents at the recruitment centres.

This is not the first time Murkomen has issued such directives. Ahead of the November 2025 intake of 10,000 constables, he similarly called for the prompt public announcement of results and threatened legal action against anyone caught paying or receiving bribes. The government has since reported recruiting a combined 13,860 officers, comprising 10,000 police constables and 3,860 prison officers.

William Ruto Secretly Travels to Congo Amid Strained Kenya-DRC Relations
items.description: President William Ruto travelled to Oyo for talks initiated by Denis Sassou Nguesso, amid strained Kenya-DRC ties, with Félix Tshisekedi expected to attend.
content: PAY ATTENTION: TUKO is in WhatsApp Channels now! Subscribe and read news in your favourite messenger.
Nancy Odindo is a Current Affairs Editor at TUKO.co.ke, covering political and world news. Odindo has over six years of journalism experience and joined TUKO.co.ke in 2023.
President William Ruto has travelled to Oyo, in the Republic of Congo, to attend a high-level four-party meeting convened by Congolese President Denis Sassou Nguesso.
The Congo government announced on Sunday, November 21, that Ruto had arrived in Oyo to participate in the gathering, which was described as a high-level diplomatic engagement initiated by Nguesso.

According to Congolese media reports, the meeting is also expected to bring together Democratic Republic of Congo President Félix Tshisekedi and Togolese Prime Minister Faure Gnassingbé, though no official confirmation of the full attendee list had been issued at the time of publication.
Ruto is reported to have left Kenya through Kisumu International Airport on Saturday after concluding a series of engagements with residents during a tour of Western Kenya .
The departure attracted attention given the low-profile nature of the trip and the diplomatic sensitivities surrounding Kenya-DRC relations.
The meeting takes place against the backdrop of a difficult period in relations between Nairobi and Kinshasa.
Tensions first escalated in December 2023 when the Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC), a political-military coalition linked to the M23 rebel movement, held a launch event in Nairobi.
The DRC government objected strongly, accusing Kenya of providing a platform to a group it regards as hostile . Kenya maintained that it had no legal basis to prevent freedom of political expression.
Photos: Babu Owino holds series of rallies in Nairobi shortly after Sifuna lands in the US

The relationship deteriorated further in October 2025 when Nairobi hosted a political meeting attended by Congolese opposition figures, among them former DRC President Joseph Kabila, drawing fresh criticism from Kinshasa.
The specific agenda of the Oyo meeting has not been officially disclosed, but its timing and composition suggest it is aimed at addressing regional security and diplomatic tensions involving the DRC.
Previously, TUKO.c.ke reported on German president Frank-Walter Steinmeier’s upcoming visit to Kenya , including his talks with Ruto and planned stops in Nairobi and Naivasha.
The visit comes as Germany seeks to deepen economic ties with Kenya, where more than 100 German companies operate.
Steinmeier’s programme will also include a tour of Crescent Island in Naivasha, focused on nature and biodiversity conservation.

items.description: Nyaliep Puot won Africa’s Next Super Model 2026 in Nairobi, earning $5,000 and global fashion opportunities as South Sudanese contestants swept the top five.
content: PAY ATTENTION: Mark TUKO.co.ke as a preferred source, and our content will appear higher in your Google feed!

Nairobi put itself firmly on the continental fashion map on Saturday, 21 November, as Broadwalk Mall came alive for the grand finale of Africa's Next Super Model 2026, a government-endorsed modelling competition that drew 20 contestants from across Africa.
South Sudan's Nyaliep Puot claimed the top prize, beating out 19 other finalists to be crowned the continent's next modelling star.
Her victory earned her a $5,000 cash prize (approximately KSh 645,000), global exposure and the chance to work with luxury international fashion brands.

The evening was a remarkable showing for South Sudan, with the country's contestants taking all five top positions.

Nyandech Changath was named first runner-up, while Nyayiel James claimed second runner-up honours.
Nyaliep succeeds Dillah Acelle, who won the 2025 edition of the competition.
For the new champion, crossing the finish line was deeply personal.
Judges were effusive in their praise, highlighting her composure and stage presence throughout the competition.
Matteo Puglisi, CEO of Select Models Management, singled her out after the final.
The grand finale opened with the Kenyan National Anthem before Joan Okorodudu, founder of the competition and CEO of Isis Models International, addressed the audience.

She thanked the Kenyan government for its endorsement and support, emphasising that such partnerships are vital for nurturing talent and strengthening Africa's creative economy.
Kenya's Ministry of Tourism and Wildlife officially backed the event, lending it significant institutional weight.
Okorodudu reflected on what the occasion meant for the continent.

The competition has built a reputation for unearthing African models who might otherwise go unrecognised on the global stage, and this year's Nairobi edition appeared to deliver on that promise in spectacular fashion.
TUKO.co.ke also highlighted facts about the World Greatness Awards 2026, which brought international leaders, royals and community figures to Nairobi for a three-day programme.
A Maasai guard of honour welcomed guests from more than 10 countries, as the ceremony recognised service and leadership through awards, knighthood investitures and Hall of Fame inductions.

Smartmatic Faces Scrutiny Over Past Election Controversies as Kenya Prepares to Replace KIEMS Kits
items.description: A company whose executives have been criminally charged by the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged bribery and money laundering schemes has…
content: A company whose executives have been criminally charged by the United States Department of Justice (DOJ) over alleged bribery and money laundering schemes has reportedly received support from prominent political figures as it seeks to remain involved in Kenya’s electoral technology procurement process ahead of the 2027 elections.

In June 2026, the Ministry of Information, Communication and the Digital Economy released a report detailing an independent technical assessment of the Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kits. The assessment reportedly recommended the decommissioning and replacement of the existing kits with newer technology designed to minimise obsolescence, reduce long-term costs and accommodate emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence.
Following the assessment, the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC) initiated a procurement process to replace the tablets supplied by Smartmatic.

Smartmatic has, however, faced legal scrutiny in the United States, where the Department of Justice announced criminal charges against the company and senior executives over allegations of conspiracy to violate the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) and international money laundering.

According to U.S. prosecutors, the alleged scheme involved approximately $1 million in bribes targeting the former chairman of the Philippine Commission on Elections (COMELEC) in connection with multi-million-dollar electoral technology contracts.

Prosecutors alleged that the scheme involved inflating the prices of voting machines and channeling excess funds through purported consulting arrangements and offshore entities in Asia, Europe and the United States to facilitate payments to corrupt officials.

The company's continued involvement in the Kenyan procurement process has also attracted political debate, with former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua publicly questioning the decision to replace the existing KIEMS technology.

Gachagua reportedly challenged the IEBC's decision to move away from Smartmatic, asking: “Why do we have to remove, to get data from a company that is already in the country and give it a new entrant? What is the gain?”

He also alleged that the proposed transition away from Smartmatic was linked to efforts to manipulate voter registers in particular regions, although the claim was not accompanied by publicly established evidence in the remarks cited.

The debate has raised questions about the influence of political interventions in procurement decisions following the technical assessment recommending the replacement of the existing electoral technology.
Concerns about Smartmatic's track record have also been raised in relation to previous elections in Kenya and other countries.

During the lead-up to Kenya's 2022 elections, three foreign Smartmatic contractors were detained at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport after reportedly carrying sensitive election deployment materials that had not been declared and were allegedly transported without official escorts.

The European Union Election Observation Mission's post-election assessment also highlighted information security weaknesses in the electoral system, including concerns over access controls and the use of shared user accounts that could potentially allow unauthorised access to system functions.

In the Philippines, Smartmatic's electoral technology has faced scrutiny following reported incidents involving corrupted SD cards ahead of the 2019 elections, alleged unauthorised script modifications during vote transmission and a reported security breach involving an employee accused of accepting bribes to facilitate third-party access to secure servers.
The Philippines subsequently barred Smartmatic from participating in its elections, according to reports cited in the allegations against the company.

Other controversies have also been linked to Smartmatic's operations internationally. In El Salvador, reported programming errors involving preferential vote calculations triggered investigations, while in Venezuela, the company's former chief executive publicly alleged that the government had manipulated voter turnout figures by more than one million.
The controversies have renewed scrutiny over the role of electoral technology suppliers, their accountability and the safeguards necessary to protect the integrity of elections.

items.title: Kenya’s new cancer rules set treatment deadlines and track SHA cover
items.description: The rules add treatment deadlines and digital tracking, but the reports leave enforcement and the system’s rollout unclear.
content: The rules add treatment deadlines and digital tracking, but the reports leave enforcement and the system’s rollout unclear.

Kenya’s 2026 cancer guidelines set deadlines for diagnosis and treatment and link cancer care to a digital system intended to track use of the Ksh800,000 SHA oncology benefit . The Ministry of Health says the rules will standardise care and improve accountability; patients have complained that delayed approvals and hospital charges can leave them without cover before treatment is complete.

The guidelines are the first major revision of Kenya’s cancer treatment protocols since 2019 . Under the new timelines, adults should receive a diagnosis within 60 days of first contact with a healthcare provider, and children within 30 days. After diagnosis, patients should be assessed at a designated or specialised cancer treatment centre within 14 days and start treatment within 31 days of registration.

The timelines are intended to cut waits across consultations, testing and referrals. The reports do not say how compliance will be measured, or what consequences facilities will face if patients miss those deadlines.

Cancer treatment will be connected to SHA’s digital oncology module. The system is intended to create a unified patient record that can be accessed across facilities, reducing duplicate records and helping care continue when patients move between hospitals. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale said it would also improve coordination and management of the oncology benefit.

Patients have raised concerns that the Ksh800,000 allocation is exhausted before treatment ends, as well as about delayed approvals, inflated bills and procedures they consider unnecessary. One patient quoted by People Daily described waiting at hospital while approval remained pending. SHA Chairman Abdi Mohamed said the authority had received complaints about questionable charges, including consultations allegedly billed when no doctor was present.

The Ministry and SHA have warned contracted facilities against using up a patient’s allocation on unnecessary services or billing for care that was not provided. The government says facilities must account for their charges. The reports do not explain how patients can challenge a bill or secure treatment when a disagreement over charges or approval arises.

The revised guidelines include molecular profiling, targeted therapy and immunotherapy—approaches the reports say were not widely embedded in the 2019 protocols. Molecular profiling examines a tumour’s genetic characteristics to help guide treatment; targeted therapy acts on particular abnormalities in cancer cells, while immunotherapy helps the immune system recognise and fight cancer.

The two People Daily accounts give slightly different estimates of the annual cancer burden: one says more than 44,000 new cases , the other says nearly 45,000. Both describe cancer as a major and growing burden. Neither provides a breakdown by cancer type, county or access to the newer treatments.

There is also no implementation timetable in the reports, nor a named body responsible for checking whether hospitals meet the new deadlines. A unified record and clearer rules may help, but the coverage does not establish whether the digital module is already operating or how quickly facilities will be connected.

Only People Daily’s account is available here, so there is no reporting from another outlet to compare against. Its two reports overlap substantially; the longer account adds direct remarks from Duale, Mohamed and a patient. The next test is whether the deadlines and billing safeguards change what patients experience at facilities—not just what the guidelines prescribe.
